paper: STALE (arXiv:2605.06527) — stale-memory / belief-update conflict benchmark: tests whether LLM memory systems detect that new observations invalidate earlier user state
scale: 400 expert-validated conflict scenarios; 1,200 evaluation probes (3 dimensions x 400 scenarios; each scored via independent judge calls); multi-turn dialogue sessions per scenario with long-context haystack up to 150K tokens per scenario. Two conflict types: Type I co-referential, Type II propagated.
construction: Hybrid: synthetic LLM generation + human expert revision. 4-step pipeline (Sec 3.4): (1) base state formulation from a hierarchical ontology of 104 attributes across 10 categories; (2) a "Logic Attacker" synthesizes conflicting observation pairs (m_old, m_new) of Type I/II; (3) a strict LLM-based quality judge validates axioms (Belief Incompatibility, Non-explicit Invalidation) with type-specific criteria — failed cases regenerated with evaluator feedback; (4) multi-turn packaging with distractor sessions drawn from LongMemEval. Gold provenance: LLM-generated then "all instances are reviewed and edited by human experts after automated generation" (Fig 2 caption); manual revision standards referenced in Appendix D.3. Construction cost ~$0.12/instance.
human_validation: Expert manual review/revision of all 400 instances (standards in Appendix D.3), but NO annotator count, NO qualifications detail, NO acceptance/pass-rate statistic, and NO inter-annotator agreement statistic (no kappa, no alpha, no percent agreement) reported anywhere for the construction-side validation. The only human-agreement number in the paper is for the downstream LLM judge (see judge field), not for dataset labels. Attention/catch checks: NONE reported (closest: pipeline rejects "syntactically obvious candidate pairs" to block shortcuts).
judge: LLM-as-judge: Gemini-3.1-flash-lite scores whether each response "demonstrates awareness of the conflict and the updated user state," judging against foundational state logic rather than reference strings; three independent judge calls per instance (one per dimension) to prevent cross-dimension leakage. Judge IS validated against humans: Appendix E.3 "Human Agreement Analysis for Automatic Evaluation" reports 95.8% agreement with human judgments and a "conservative bias" (Limitations, App A: judge "may still miss nuanced correct responses"). However, the sample size and annotator count of that agreement study are not stated in the HTML body, and no kappa is given — only percent agreement. Main metric: accuracy (%), broken down by conflict type x dimension (Table 2).
quality_controls: (a) Distractor/leakage: distractor sessions from LongMemEval are "conservatively filtered to exclude content that could plausibly update the target state," ensuring m_new is the sole conflict source for the target attribute; (b) shortcut control: rejection of syntactically obvious conflict pairs; (c) judge-call independence: three independent calls per instance to prevent information leakage across dimensions; (d) axiom-based LLM validation of every generated pair (Belief Incompatibility, Non-explicit Invalidation). ABSENT: parametric-knowledge / contamination check against pretraining data; ablations of the benchmark itself (e.g., difficulty knobs, distractor-count sweeps).
splits: NONE reported. HF release is a single "train" split containing all 400 rows — no dev/test split, no held-out set, no multi-seed or multi-version policy; runs-per-system, seeds, and temperature settings not stated in the extracted text.
baselines: 14 systems: 5 closed-source LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5.4-nano, GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1-flash-lite, Gemini-3.1-pro), 4 open-source LLMs (Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-27B, MiniMax-M2.5), 5 memory frameworks (LightMem, Zep, LiCoMemory, A-mem, mem0), plus the authors' prototype CUPMem. Score range on overall accuracy: best Gemini-3.1-pro 55.2%, worst Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct 2.6%.
cost_reporting: Partial. Dollar costs: benchmark construction ~$0.12/instance; per-instance evaluation cost for some frameworks (LightMem ~$0.02, A-MEM ~$0.38, CUPMem ~$0.37). NONE reported: token counts of evaluated systems, latency/wall-clock.
release: Public on HuggingFace: STALEproj/STALE — 400 rows, single train split, 306 MB, auto-converted to Parquet, ~334 downloads/month. License: CC BY 4.0 (stated in paper and on HF card). Dataset card documents fields (uid, M_old, M_new, explanation, probing_queries, haystack_session, relevant_session_index, timestamps, type) but no formal datasheet (Gebru-style) and no GitHub link on the HF page; paper's Appendix G "Code and Dataset Access" exists but its URL content was not retrievable from the HTML, so a code repo is unconfirmed.
notable_practices: Practices a new benchmark paper is expected to match, exemplified here: (1) validating the LLM judge against human labels and reporting the agreement number (95.8%) plus its bias direction ("conservative"); (2) reporting construction AND per-system evaluation dollar cost per instance; (3) explicit anti-leakage design statements (filtered distractors, sole-conflict-source guarantee, independent judge calls per dimension); (4) axiom-style formal criteria for what counts as a valid item, with regenerate-on-fail loop; (5) dedicated Limitations appendix acknowledging judge failure modes; (6) permissive CC BY 4.0 release with a field-documented HF dataset card. Gaps worth noting for contrast: no inter-annotator agreement on construction, no judge-validation sample size, no dev/test split, no seed/variance policy, no contamination check.

paper: LoCoMo — "Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents" (arXiv:2402.17753, Maharana et al., Snap Research + UNC, ACL 2024)
scale: 50 machine-generated dyadic conversations; avg 19.3 sessions per conversation (up to 35), avg 304.9 turns, avg 9,209.2 tokens per conversation, avg 32.3 shared images per conversation. Three tasks: (1) QA — 7,512 questions total across 5 categories (single-hop 2,705; multi-hop 1,104; temporal 1,547; open-domain 285; adversarial 1,871 = 14.6%... adversarial share stated as ~14.6% of benchmark); (2) event summarization — event-graph ground truth averaging 24.2 events per conversation; (3) multimodal dialogue generation. NOTE: the public GitHub release (locomo10.json) contains only 10 of the 50 conversations — README: subset sampled "to retain the longest conversations with high-quality annotations and for cost-effective evaluation of closed-source LLMs."
construction: Hybrid: machine-generated then human-edited. Pipeline (Sec. 3): (a) personas expanded from the MSC dataset via gpt-3.5-turbo (Sec. 3.1); (b) temporal event graphs of up to 25 causally-connected events spanning 6-12 months per speaker, generated iteratively (Sec. 3.2); (c) two LLM-based generative agents converse using a "reflect & respond" memory mechanism (session summaries as short-term memory, observation assertions as long-term memory) plus image-sharing/image-reaction behaviors (Sec. 3.3). Human editing pass (Sec. 3.4): annotators edited ~15% of dialog turns and removed/substituted ~19% of images to fix long-term inconsistencies, verify grounding to event graphs, and remove irrelevant images. Gold provenance: QA answers "directly taken from conversations as much as possible" with supporting turn IDs annotated by humans (Sec. 4.1); event-summarization gold = the temporal event graphs themselves (Sec. 4.2).
human_validation: Human involvement is in-the-loop editing/annotation, not an independent validation study. No inter-annotator agreement statistics (no kappa, no percent agreement) reported anywhere. Protocol: in-house annotators followed an editing checklist (Appendix A.3: remove irrelevant images, add missing context, replace mismatched images, edit for cross-session consistency, align with event graphs); reported outcomes are edit rates (~15% of turns edited, ~19% of images removed/substituted, Sec. 3.4). Number of annotators: NOT reported; Appendix B.3 states annotators were in-house and demographics could not be obtained "due to the confidential nature." No catch trials / attention checks reported.
judge: No LLM judge for QA in the paper: QA scored by lexical F1 ("F1 score for exact matches" after answer normalization; F1 partial match; Sec. 4.1), plus recall@k for retrieval accuracy of RAG variants; adversarial category scored on whether the model identifies questions as unanswerable. Event summarization scored with an adapted FactScore (precision/recall over atomic facts vs. event-graph facts — LLM-assisted fact decomposition inherited from FactScore) plus ROUGE-1/2/L (Sec. 4.2). Multimodal dialogue: MMRelevance, BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore (Sec. 4.3). No validation of any automatic/LLM-based scorer against human labels is reported. (Caveat for gap analysis: the widely-used GPT-4/LLM-as-judge LoCoMo protocol comes from later third-party work, e.g. Mem0/Zep, not from this paper.)
quality_controls: Adversarial question category (1,871 questions, ~14.6%) designed to trick models into answering unanswerable questions — the main built-in distractor control (Sec. 4.1). Human editing pass against event-graph grounding acts as a consistency control (Sec. 3.4). Contamination / parametric-knowledge-leak checks: NONE reported (data is synthetic-persona generated, which implicitly limits contamination, but no explicit check is run). Benchmark self-ablations: NONE reported; Appendix D.1's five-way error taxonomy for summarization (missing info, hallucination, dialog-cue misunderstanding, speaker attribution, saliency) is post-hoc error analysis, not a construction-time control.
splits: No dev/test split for the QA and summarization tasks — all 50 conversations are evaluation data. For multimodal dialogue generation, 50 additional unfiltered pipeline-generated conversations are used as training data (Sec. 5, Appendix C.1). No held-out set, no versioning policy. Single inference run per model — "we report results from a single inference run for each model" (Appendix C.2); no seeds/variance reported.
baselines: ~5 base LLMs plus retrieval variants: Mistral-7B, Llama-2-70B-Chat, gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4-turbo (QA); long-context gpt-3.5-turbo-16k; RAG = DRAGON retriever + gpt-3.5-turbo-16k reader with three retrieval-source conditions (raw dialog turns, observations, session summaries) at varying top-k. Multimodal dialogue: MiniGPT-5 base / +summary / +observation. Human performance reported as reference on QA (humans far exceed all models). No commercial memory systems evaluated.
cost_reporting: Essentially NONE for evaluated systems: dataset-side token statistics are reported (avg 9,209.2 tokens/conversation; Table 5), and cost is invoked qualitatively (the GitHub subset was sampled for "cost-effective evaluation of closed-source LLMs"), but no dollar cost, per-system token consumption, or latency numbers for any evaluated model/configuration.
release: Public: project page https://snap-research.github.io/locomo, code+data at https://github.com/snap-research/locomo. License: CC BY-NC 4.0 (Appendix B.2; LICENSE.txt in repo = Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International, non-commercial use only). Released data = data/locomo10.json with 10 of the 50 conversations (longest, high-quality-annotation subset); QA eval scripts for OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini/HF models and RAG released; event summarization and multimodal-dialogue eval code marked "Coming soon" in README. No HuggingFace dataset page from the authors, no formal datasheet (appendices carry prompts, statistics, and editing examples instead).
notable_practices: Practices this paper exemplifies that a new benchmark paper is expected to match: (1) explicit question typology with per-category counts (single-hop / multi-hop / temporal / open-domain / adversarial) and per-category result breakdowns; (2) a built-in adversarial/unanswerable category to measure abstention rather than only recall; (3) gold answers grounded to evidence turn IDs, enabling retrieval-recall@k evaluation separate from answer F1; (4) quantified human post-editing of machine-generated data (reporting the 15%-of-turns / 19%-of-images edit rates); (5) generation grounded in an explicit temporal event graph that doubles as summarization ground truth; (6) human performance ceiling reported for QA; (7) full generative prompts and annotation checklist released in appendices; (8) clear license (CC BY-NC 4.0). Expected practices it lacks (gap-relevant): inter-annotator agreement, judge-vs-human validation, contamination checks, multi-seed runs, cost/latency reporting, and a full-data release (only 10/50 conversations public).

paper: LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory — Wu, Wang, Yu, Zhang, Chang, Yu (arXiv:2410.10813, ICLR 2025)
scale: 500 manually curated questions across 7 types (single-session-user, single-session-assistant, single-session-preference, multi-session reasoning, knowledge-update, temporal-reasoning, plus 30 false-premise/abstention questions derived from the other types; per-type counts for the full 500 are NOT reported in the paper text). Two haystack settings: LongMemEval_S ≈ 50 sessions / ~115k tokens per problem; LongMemEval_M ≈ 500 sessions / ~1.5M tokens. Per-session turn/token averages: NONE reported. A third variant, LongMemEval_Oracle (evidence sessions only, ground-truth retrieval), is released in the repo.
construction: Hybrid synthetic-with-heavy-human-curation. User attributes drawn from a 164-attribute ontology in 5 categories; user backgrounds LLM-generated (Llama 3 70B). Questions initially proposed by Llama 3 70B (all types) + GPT-4o (temporal/multi-session/preference), then human-filtered/rewritten at ~5% yield (~1000 candidates screened per type). Answers manually decomposed into evidence statements with timestamps; annotators assigned session positions/timestamps. Evidence chat sessions are LLM self-chat (user-LLM vs assistant-LLM) with ~70% manually edited; manual screening checked evidence inclusion, position distribution, natural phrasing (Sec 3.2). Haystack filler: 25% ShareGPT + 25% UltraChat + 50% simulated sessions, with evidence sessions randomly inserted mid-history.
human_validation: Three expert annotators with "more than three years of NLP research experience"; ~400 human hours on dataset construction + ~150 hours on the commercial-system study (Ethics Statement). Uncertain cases resolved by discussion among annotators. NO inter-annotator agreement statistic (no kappa, no percent agreement) reported for the dataset construction itself. No mention of catch/attention checks.
judge: LLM-as-judge: GPT-4o-2024-08-06 via OpenAI API with prompt-engineered, per-question-type prompts (separate prompts to handle edge cases). Judge IS validated against humans: a meta-evaluation on 30 questions per question type reports ">97% agreement with human experts" (Sec 3.3; per-category agreement in Table 6, Appendix A.4). Meta-eval covered judging outputs of both GPT-4o and Llama 3.1 8B systems.
quality_controls: Distractors explicitly constructed: irrelevant sessions sampled from ShareGPT/UltraChat plus simulated sessions on non-conflicting attributes; evidence sessions randomly positioned to control position bias. Abstention control: 30 false-premise questions testing refusal on unknown information. Benchmark-difficulty validation: commercial assistants (ChatGPT/Coze) drop 37%/64% even on ~10x-shortened histories; long-context LLMs drop 30-60% on LongMemEval_S (Sec 3.4, Fig 3). Contamination/parametric-leak checks: NONE reported. Post-release quality maintenance: Sept 2025 "longmemeval-cleaned" HF release removed history sessions interfering with answer correctness, with change logs.
splits: NONE reported — no dev/test split, no held-out set, no multi-seed policy. All 500 questions form a single evaluation set, offered in three configurations (S, M, Oracle). Versioning exists only as post-hoc dataset cleanup (Sept 2025 cleaned release on HuggingFace with change logs).
baselines: Three families: (1) 2 commercial assistant products x 2 backbone configs — ChatGPT (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini) and Coze (GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-turbo), evaluated on a 97-question subset with short 3-6-session histories; (2) 5 long-context LLMs — GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 Instruct 70B and 8B, Phi-3 14B (128k), Phi-3.5 Mini 4B — reading the full haystack; (3) memory-system ablations over the benchmark's own design space: value granularity (session/round/summary/fact), key expansion (fact/keyphrase), time-aware vs naive query expansion, reading strategies (direct, Chain-of-Note, JSON vs NL) — 9+ retriever/reader/index configurations total.
cost_reporting: NONE reported — no token counts, dollar cost, or latency figures for evaluated systems in the paper (retrieval metrics like Recall@k are reported instead; the repo ships print_retrieval_metrics.py but no cost accounting).
release: Public. GitHub: github.com/xiaowu0162/LongMemEval (MIT license) with evaluation scripts (evaluate_qa.py with GPT-4o judge, print_qa_metrics.py, print_retrieval_metrics.py), dataset-format documentation, and instructions for compiling custom histories. HuggingFace: xiaowu0162/longmemeval-cleaned (Sept 2025 cleaned version). Google Drive links for corpus/timestamped-event files. Source-data licenses: Apache 2.0 (ShareGPT), MIT (UltraChat). No formal datasheet, but field-level format docs + change logs are provided.
notable_practices: (1) Judge meta-validation with a number attached: per-type human agreement study (30 q/type, >97%, Table 6) — the practice reviewers now expect for any LLM-judged benchmark. (2) Oracle-retrieval variant shipped alongside S/M, cleanly decoupling retrieval failure from reading failure. (3) Explicit abstention/false-premise subset so refusal is measured, not just accuracy. (4) Controlled distractor injection with randomized evidence position at two haystack scales (115k vs 1.5M tokens), making difficulty attributable to history length. (5) Ethics-statement disclosure of annotation labor (3 experts, ~400+150 hours) and yield rate (~5%) — documents curation intensity. (6) Post-publication dataset maintenance: versioned cleaned re-release with change logs. Gaps a new benchmark should improve on: no inter-annotator kappa, no per-type question counts in the paper, no dev/test split, no contamination check, no cost/latency reporting.

paper: MemConflict: Evaluating Long-Term Memory Systems Under Memory Conflicts (arXiv:2605.20926, cs.IR, submitted 2026-05-20; authors Zhen Tao, Jinxiang Zhao, Peng Liu, Dinghao Xi, Yanfang Chen, Wei Xu, Zhiyu Li). Diagnostic benchmark treating memory validity as query-conditioned fitness-for-use across three conflict types: dynamic (temporal validity), static (factual correctness), conditional (contextual applicability).
scale: 12 benchmark instances (each = one virtual user; Sec 3.7, Table 2). Per instance averages: 52.33 sessions, 2,349.17 dialogue turns, 203,910.83 tokens, 124.33 evaluation queries (90.82 dynamic / 16.65 static / 16.86 conditional), 32.83 distractor entries. Controlled conflict distances: dynamic 5–25 sessions, static 10–45, conditional 9–49 (Table 2). Totals therefore roughly ~628 sessions and ~1,492 queries across the whole benchmark.
construction: Fully synthetic (Sec 3). Structured user profiles with five components — invariant attributes, dynamic states, conditional preferences, personality traits/goals, related entities — seeded from Persona Hub and expanded by an LLM (Sec 3.2, Eq. 2). Conflicts injected programmatically: dynamic via LLM-proposed state-update trajectories validated against feasibility/cooldown/persona constraints (Sec 3.3.2, Eq. 5); static via a true value at session p plus a later non-update contradiction at session q (Sec 3.3.3); conditional via multiple condition–value pairs for the same attribute across sessions (Sec 3.3.4); distractors drawn from related-entity information within conflict spans (Sec 3.3.5). Dialogues generated in two stages (LLM synopsis then multi-turn expansion) with the requirement that every non-empty information item be explicitly realized (Sec 3.4). Gold provenance is benchmark-defined by construction: query-conditioned validity with a guaranteed unique maximizer per query (Sec 3.1, Eq. 1). All construction LLM calls use gpt-5.0-mini (Sec 4.2).
human_validation: Qualitative only, no statistics. Two touchpoints: (1) construction — "Human experts inspect the dialogues for naturalness, coherence, and information coverage" and verify items are explicitly expressed and correctly attributed (Sec 3.4); (2) scoring — "All answer and memory-item judgments are produced through LLM-assisted matching followed by human verification. Human annotators review the LLM judgments, especially ambiguous matches, paraphrases, and attribution cases" (Sec 3.6). NONE reported for: number of annotators, inter-annotator agreement (no kappa, no percent agreement), sample sizes checked, correction rates, annotation guidelines, attention/catch checks.
judge: LLM-assisted matching (gpt-5.0-mini, Sec 4.2) followed by human verification of judgments, with final metrics computed from verified judgments (Sec 3.6). The LLM judge is NOT validated against human labels — no judge-vs-human agreement numbers anywhere in the paper. Metrics: black-box Answer Accuracy (Eq. 11), Update Order Consistency Score (Eq. 14, dynamic only), Conflict Recognition Score (Eq. 15, static only); white-box Support Evidence Hit@K (Eq. 12) and Support Rank Score (log-discounted rank, Eq. 13), all in Sec 3.6.
quality_controls: Construction-time controls: attribute-specific validation rules enforcing feasibility, cooldown, and persona-consistency constraints on state updates (Sec 3.3.2, Eq. 5); conflict isolation — target attributes not re-mentioned in intervening sessions (Secs 3.3.3–3.3.4); semantically similar related-entity distractors injected deliberately (Sec 3.3.5); human expert inspection of dialogue naturalness/coverage/attribution (Sec 3.4); unique-maximizer guarantee for every query's gold answer (Sec 3.1). Benchmark-design sensitivity ablations vary retrieval depth, dialogue length, distractor injection, query formulation, and conflict distance (Sec 4.4; Ablation/ directory in repo). NONE reported: contamination or parametric-knowledge-leak checks (though fully synthetic personas reduce, without demonstrating absence of, parametric leakage).
splits: NONE reported: no dev/test split, no held-out set, no multi-seed or multi-run protocol (results appear single-run), no versioning policy. The full set of 12 instances is the evaluation set.
baselines: Six long-term memory systems: A-Mem, LangMem, Letta, MemOS, Mem0, Memobase (Sec 4). All use gpt-5.0-mini as the backbone for LLM calls (Sec 4.2). No non-memory baselines (no long-context-only or vanilla-RAG arm) are evaluated. Headline finding: uneven strengths across conflict types, with answer correctness often diverging from supporting-memory retrieval/ranking.
cost_reporting: Partial — latency yes, tokens/$ no. Table 6 (Sec 4.5.1) reports per-system Addition Time (472.67–40,215.80 s), Retrieval Time (2.23–471.15 s), Response Time (813.86–1,344.09 s), and Total Runtime (1,356.30–41,210.83 s); e.g., MemOS achieves lowest total runtime. NONE reported for token counts or dollar cost of evaluated systems.
release: Public at https://github.com/TaoZhen1110/MemConflict (linked from abstract; repo created 2026-05-16, last push 2026-06-27, 12 stars). Release includes: main benchmark file Data/Step4_4.jsonl (multi-session histories, conflict metadata, queries, gold labels, black-/white-box eval fields), intermediate Step files for construction transparency, full construction pipeline (run_construction_pipeline.py), per-system evaluation scripts for all six baselines, Ablation/ scripts, and full prompts in Prompt/. NONE reported: repository license (GitHub API license field is null), datasheet/data card, HuggingFace mirror, ethics statement. arXiv page carries only the standard arXiv perpetual non-exclusive license.
notable_practices: Practices this paper exemplifies that a new benchmark paper is expected to match: (1) dual-mode evaluation — black-box final-answer scoring plus white-box supporting-evidence retrieval/ranking metrics (SEH@K, SRS), enabling diagnosis of where systems fail rather than only whether; (2) per-conflict-type taxonomy with dedicated metrics per type (UOCS for dynamic, CRS for static) and per-type result breakdowns; (3) explicit controlled construction parameters reported in a dataset-statistics table (conflict distances, distractor counts, tokens/turns/sessions per instance); (4) benchmark-design sensitivity ablations (dialogue length, distractor injection, query style, conflict distance, retrieval depth) shipped with code; (5) full construction-pipeline release including intermediate artifacts and all prompts, making the generator reproducible and auditable; (6) per-phase latency reporting (add/retrieve/respond) for every evaluated system; (7) gold labels guaranteed unique by construction (unique-maximizer property). Its main omissions — no annotator counts/kappa, no judge-vs-human validation numbers, no seeds/splits, no repo license, no cost-in-dollars — are equally instructive as gap-analysis anchors.

paper: PrecisionMemBench — "Structured Belief State and the First Precision-Aware Benchmark for LLM Memory Retrieval" (arXiv:2605.11325, Jeffrey Flynt / TenureHQ; paper page license CC BY 4.0)
scale: 89 scored cases = 77 single-turn + 12 turn-level assertions across 2 session scenarios. Single-turn breakdown: 43 active-retrieval passes, 25 structural passes, 9 trivially-empty passes. Underlying corpus: 35-belief seed (23 code-scoped, 7 writing-scoped, 5 universal) plus a secondary-user fixture (Seed Corpus section). 15 case categories (Table 2). Main session scenario: opens on a topic, drifts across 8 unrelated turns, returns at turns 9–10 with new surface forms. Tokens per item: NONE reported.
construction: Fully synthetic, specification-authored (no natural data, no LLM-generation pipeline reported). A hand-built 35-belief seed with "controlled collisions" over overlapping names, scope, lifecycle state, supersession, relations, and cross-user isolation. Gold provenance: each case is a declarative spec — requesting user, active scope(s), natural-language query, optional belief budget, and expected belief IDs via three assertion types: mustInclude, mustExclude, shouldOnlyInclude (Evaluation section). Gold = author-specified belief-ID sets by construction, not annotated post hoc.
human_validation: NONE reported. No human annotation of cases or outputs, no annotator counts, no kappa/percent-agreement statistics, no attention/catch checks. Gold labels are author-specified case expectations; correctness of the gold sets themselves is not independently validated.
judge: No LLM judge. Scoring is deterministic belief-ID matching on retrieved IDs before answer generation — paper explicitly frames this as "separating retrieval behavior from downstream model and judge behavior" (Evaluation section). Metrics: precision/recall over query-dependent belief IDs (active-assertion cases); drift score = fraction of retrieved non-pinned beliefs originating in off-topic turns, 0 = perfect isolation (Table 5); latency in ms. Judge-vs-human validation: moot/absent — there is no LLM judge and no human labels to validate against.
quality_controls: Distractor/adversarial design: controlled collisions in the seed corpus; explicit boundary categories — alias resolution, scope disambiguation, supersession chain exclusion, fuzzy matching and prefix guards, counter-signal retrieval, cross-user isolation, budget eviction, ranking stability, session-level noise isolation under topic drift. Reproducibility control: every evaluated provider pinned to a public revision, binary, or container digest; configurations that cannot be pinned or that alter ranking/thresholds/fixtures excluded. NO contamination or parametric-knowledge-leak checks (synthetic IDs make classic contamination less applicable, but no discussion), NO ablations of the benchmark itself, NO paraphrase-robustness or multi-seed variance analysis, no dedicated Limitations section (closest: results are "reproducible measurements of specific versions and configurations, not permanent judgments").
splits: NONE reported. Single unified 89-case suite; no dev/test split, no held-out set, no multi-seed or benchmark-versioning policy in the paper (repo shows a main branch with 31 commits, no formal release tags visible).
baselines: 13 system configurations, all memory/retrieval systems (not raw LLMs): Tenure (authors' own system: 43/43 active passes, mean precision 1.00), Open Knowledge Format (18 passes, 0.47), Supermemory (4 passes, 0.22), Gbrain (5 passes, 0.14), plus YourMemory, Cognee, A-MEM, AtomicMemory, Hindsight, Mem0, Zep, AgentMemory, and a Vector baseline (each 0–5 active passes, mean precision 0.05–0.17). Note: the top system is the paper's own contribution.
cost_reporting: Latency: yes, per-system in ms (Table 5 session latency: Tenure 47.8, Open Knowledge Format 3349.5, YourMemory 430.5, Supermemory 172.3, Vector baseline 256.8, A-MEM 25.7); ingestion latency also reported (Hindsight 672.15 ms single-turn retrieval, 173.3 s to ingest the 35-belief corpus; Zep 139.64 ms retrieval but 897.0 s ingestion, individual beliefs up to 125,148 ms to become available). Token counts and dollar costs: NONE reported.
release: Public. Benchmark repo: github.com/tenurehq/precisionmembench (MIT license; harness needs Node.js 20+ and Docker, run via `npx ava src/retrieval.external.eval.test.ts` with MEMORY_PROVIDER env vars; per-case baseline reports with precision/recall/latency committed to test-results/baseline/). System code: github.com/tenurehq/tenure. HF dataset: huggingface.co/datasets/tenurehq/precisionmembench; HF Spaces leaderboard: huggingface.co/spaces/tenurehq/precisionmembench. Paper on arXiv under CC BY 4.0. No formal datasheet; README serves as documentation.
notable_practices: (1) Deterministic ID-level scoring upstream of answer generation — eliminates LLM-judge noise entirely and isolates retrieval from generation. (2) Negative assertions as first-class gold (mustExclude / shouldOnlyInclude) so precision failures cannot be masked by dumping the whole store. (3) Version-pinning discipline: every evaluated provider pinned to a public revision/binary/container digest, unpinnable configs excluded, and results explicitly framed as version-specific measurements. (4) Per-case machine-readable baseline reports committed in-repo plus an HF leaderboard. (5) Latency reported alongside accuracy, including ingestion-to-availability latency. Counterpoint gaps a report-card reader should note: zero human validation, no dev/test split, no benchmark self-ablation, and the author's own system defines the ceiling (1.00) on their own benchmark.

paper: MemOps: Benchmarking Lifecycle Memory Operations in Long-Horizon Conversations (arXiv:2607.12893; Hao, Zhang, Lin et al.; MemTensor). Note: the "403 instances" in the task refers to 403 evidence conversations; the paper counts 4,012 evaluation instances.
scale: 403 evidence conversations (retained from 727 generated), each with 3 segments of 8 alternating turns → 1,209 segments / 9,672 dialogue turns; 2,006 unique QA pairs, each probed under 2 settings (adjacent-evidence and long-context) → 4,012 evaluation instances (Sec 3.4, Table 2). Avg 4.0 operations per trajectory; 100 unique topics; 5 operation families (Remember, Forget, Update, Reflect, TrajectoryOps) in comparable proportions (Fig 5a); 6 probe categories (OperationTrace, TargetBinding, StateTransition, CandidateDisambiguation, OperationApplication, StateTrajectory; Sec 3.2). Tokens per item: ~2,557 avg in adjacent setting; 60,821 avg / 68,309 max in long-context setting (Table 2).
construction: Fully synthetic, LLM-generated via a 4-stage pipeline (Sec 3.2): (1) topic-specific user-profile/background construction; (2) evidence-conversation + gold operation-trace generation (5 dialogues per topic, one per operation type); (3) operation-level probe (QA) generation; (4) long-context construction by embedding evidence conversations into unrelated UltraChat dialogue pools with inserted distractors. Gold provenance: gold traces and answers come from the generation pipeline itself, not human annotation; each operation must carry a trigger span and supporting evidence whose quoted text appears verbatim in user turns. The paper does NOT name the generator LLM used to produce the data.
human_validation: NONE reported. No human annotation, human audit, annotator counts, agreement statistics (no kappa/percent agreement), or catch checks anywhere in the paper. All quality assurance is automated (deterministic gates + LLM verifier, Sec 3.3). The conclusion (Sec 5) explicitly names "stronger human validation and judge-calibration studies, especially for provenance and reflection quality" as future work — i.e., the authors acknowledge the absence.
judge: LLM-as-judge: GPT-4o compares each model response against the gold operation trace, gold provenance, and evidence conversation, assigning binary labels for the applicable metrics (Sec 4.1). Six reported metrics: Answer Accuracy, Operation F1, Provenance Support, Leakage Rate, Stale Value Rate, Reflect Precision (Tables 3-5, broken down by system, operation type, probe category). The judge is NOT validated against human labels — no human-judge agreement numbers or calibration study; acknowledged as a limitation in Sec 5.
quality_controls: Two-layer automated pipeline (Sec 3.3): deterministic local gates enforcing strict structural/schema constraints, then an LLM verifier auditing dialogue grounding, operation-trace integrity, state-transition consistency, probe-coverage, and leakage of internal labels into surface text. Retention rate reported: 727 generated → 403 retained (55.4%, Table 2). Distractor design: operation-aware, state-neutral "context-level distractors" derived from the gold trace and semantically close to the target memory, avg 5.7 per sample (Sec 3.2 Stage 4, Fig 5c), plus unrelated UltraChat filler. NO contamination check on evaluated models (e.g., no closed-book/parametric-only-answering control) and NO ablations of the benchmark itself (no evidence-removal or shuffling controls) reported.
splits: NONE reported. No dev/test split, no held-out set, no multi-seed or multi-version policy, no regeneration policy. The adjacent vs long-context pairing of the same 2,006 QA pairs is an experimental condition, not a data split. Also no reported seeds/temperature/run counts for evaluated systems (Sec 4.1 omits them).
baselines: 11 systems across 4 paradigms (Sec 4.1, Table 3): 7 long-context LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1-mini, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, Gemini-3-Flash, GLM-4.6, Qwen3.6-27B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash); 1 RAG system (BM25 retriever + GPT-4.1-mini at turn- and session-level granularity); 1 parametric-memory method (Temp-LoRA); 2 managed memory systems (Mem0, MemOS). Headline numbers: best adjacent-setting Claude-Sonnet-4.5 at 0.916 accuracy / 0.941 provenance support; best long-context GLM-4.6 at 0.808 accuracy; worst Temp-LoRA at 0.162 accuracy (Table 3).
cost_reporting: NONE reported. Table 3 carries accuracy and diagnostic metrics only — no token counts, dollar cost, or latency figures for any evaluated system, and no cost comparison between memory systems and long-context baselines.
release: Public code on GitHub (github.com/MemTensor/MemOps), MIT license. Repo contains the full 5-stage generation pipeline and evaluation scripts (5-test_operation_metrics.py, 5.5-evaluate_operation_metrics.py) and generated artifacts through the injection stage — but the final 403-conversation / 2,006-QA benchmark dataset itself is NOT shipped: users must regenerate it via external LLM APIs plus a separately downloaded UltraChat corpus. No Hugging Face dataset release, no formal datasheet; documentation is a README covering design, operation families, difficulty knobs, and JSON data format. Generation and judge prompts are not reproduced in the paper's appendix.
notable_practices: Practices this paper exemplifies that a new benchmark paper is expected to have: (1) reporting the generation-pipeline retention rate (727→403, 55.4%) rather than hiding filtering; (2) a full dataset-statistics table (Table 2: turns, segments, ops/trajectory, avg/max token lengths per setting); (3) an operation-level diagnostic metric suite beyond final-answer accuracy (leakage rate, stale-value rate, provenance support) enabling failure-mode diagnosis; (4) a verbatim-provenance requirement — every gold operation tied to quoted text that must appear in user turns — making labels mechanically auditable; (5) paired evaluation of identical QA pairs in adjacent vs long-context settings, isolating the context-length effect; (6) reported distractor composition statistics (avg 5.7 operation-aware distractors/sample, Fig 5c); (7) an explicit limitation statement flagging missing human validation and judge calibration. Its gaps (no human validation, unvalidated judge, no cost reporting, no splits, dataset not directly shipped) are equally instructive as anti-patterns for the gap analysis.

paper: ChronoScope — "Evaluating Temporal Consistency in Multi-Turn Language Models" (Yash Kumar Atri, Steven L. Johnson, Tom Hartvigsen; arXiv:2604.23051, submitted 2026-04-24; accepted at ACL 2026)
scale: 1,469,628 interaction chains (Sec 3.1, Table 2), 2–11 turns per chain (median 2, mean 2.27); >1.4M evaluated turns total. 11 chain families (Table 2): Carryover 552,408; Carryover-then 324,637; Scope switch 233,098; Cross-entity then 144,618; Multi-turn chain 72,009; Temporal narrative 30,335; Interval reasoning 30,335; Interval change 27,655; Distinct count 27,655; Change point 24,357; Bridged multi-pid 2,521 (counts sum exactly to 1,469,628). Experiments sample "up to 100,000 chains from each stratum" (App B). Tokens per item: NONE reported.
construction: Fully synthetic, deterministically generated from structured data — "constructed deterministically from Wikidata snapshots and contains no human-written or model-generated content" (Sec 3.2). Gold provenance: 4 yearly Wikidata snapshots (2022–2025) with quarterly temporal anchors; truth tables materialized from start/end/point-in-time qualifiers, deduplicated by Wikidata rank (preferred > normal) (Sec 3.2, App B.1). Questions rendered via fixed, property-specific templates parameterized by question type. Hygiene filters remove deprecated statements, self-loops, identifiers, malformed strings, duplicates (App B.1.2–B.1.3). A paraphrased variant of 10,000 chains was generated with gpt-5-2025-08-07 (preserving entities/dates/answers) for the robustness study (Table 5). Domains: politics, business, sports, academia, public institutions.
human_validation: NONE reported. No annotators, no kappa/percent agreement, no attention checks anywhere in main text or appendices. The paper's implicit justification is determinism: "Given fixed truth tables, templates, and random seeds, this generation process is fully deterministic," with gold answers taken directly from Wikidata. Note: no human spot-check of template naturalness/answerability or of the exact-match scorer is reported either.
judge: No LLM judge. Scoring is a "normalized exact-match procedure": normalizes whitespace/punctuation, strips common answer prefixes (e.g., "Answer:"), allows exact or substring match after normalization (App B.4); auxiliary token-level and character-level F1 also reported. A separate Drift metric counts present-day-answer substitutions vs. the historical gold (Sec 4.1, App B.4). The automated scorer is NOT validated against human labels — no agreement numbers of any kind. GPT-5 is used only to paraphrase questions for the Table 5 robustness study, not to score.
quality_controls: No explicit contamination or parametric-leak check (Wikidata is public; the paper does not test held-out snapshots or memorization controls). Partial mitigations: (1) paraphrase robustness ablation — 10,000 chains rewritten by gpt-5-2025-08-07, "results remain largely consistent across both versions" (Table 5, Sec 5), addressing template surface-form artifacts; (2) the Drift metric itself operationalizes the parametric present-day-knowledge confound as a measured quantity; (3) stratified benchmark analyses by chain family, chain length, and follow-up position (App B.3, Tables 6–9); (4) label hygiene filters (App B.1). No distractors (open-ended answers, not multiple choice).
splits: No explicit dev/test split or held-out set defined in the paper. Evaluation uses stratified sampling (up to 100,000 chains per stratum) with "randomness ... limited to chain sampling and ... controlled via fixed seeds" (App B, Determinism); "all evaluations are deterministic given model outputs and Wikidata-derived gold answers." The reproducibility statement says "dataset splits" are among released artifacts (App A.1), but the paper does not define them. No multi-seed model runs or benchmark-versioning policy reported; snapshot years (2022–2025) provide implicit versioning.
baselines: ~10 models (Sec 4.1, App A.1), each under three settings (Gold Context / Self-Conditioned / Questions Only). Named: open-weight — Qwen-2.5-7B, Qwen-3-4B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-7B, DeepSeek-V3; proprietary — ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Gemini-2.5-Flash (model names as written in the paper). Additional models tested but omitted from main tables as underperforming: LLaMA-3 variants, Phi-3, Phi-4, NVIDIA Nemotron (App A.1). No agentic/memory-augmented systems — plain LMs only.
cost_reporting: NONE reported — no token counts, dollar costs, or latency for any evaluated system.
release: Public. Code: https://github.com/yashkumaratri/ChronoScope (Apache 2.0; evaluation script hf_scope_benchmark.py, data-pipeline utilities, SLURM templates; currently 0 stars, 7 commits). Data: HuggingFace dataset yashkumaratri/ChronoScope, downloadable as merged_scope_benchmark.jsonl via huggingface-cli. arXiv page under CC BY 4.0. Released artifacts per App A.1: prompt templates, evaluation scripts, dataset splits, metadata. No formal datasheet — documentation is the README's 11-family taxonomy plus Appendices A–B.
notable_practices: (1) Fully deterministic, seed-controlled generation and scoring enabling exact replication ("fully deterministic given model outputs and gold answers"); (2) internally consistent bookkeeping — per-family counts sum exactly to the reported total; (3) a three-setting protocol (Gold Context / Self-Conditioned / Questions Only) that separates scope-tracking ability from error propagation and gives an explicit lower bound; (4) a named failure-mode metric (Drift = present-day substitution rate) rather than accuracy alone; (5) a paraphrase-robustness ablation of the benchmark itself to rule out template artifacts; (6) stratified reporting by chain family/length/turn position; (7) versioned gold via dated Wikidata snapshots, making the benchmark refreshable. Conversely, it exemplifies the pattern where deterministic KG grounding is used to argue human validation and judge calibration away entirely — a report-card gap a new benchmark paper can differentiate against.

paper: "Can Agent Memory Systems Track Evolving State?" — Xinyi Fan, Miri Liu, Ruozhen Yang, Siru Ouyang, Jiawei Han; arXiv:2608.19652, submitted 2026-08-20. Introduces StateMemBench (benchmark) and StateMem (method; state-first memory wrapper, 1.8x current-state accuracy over strongest baseline on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, 1.6x on Qwen-3.5-9B).
scale: 234 multi-session scenarios in two length regimes: Set A (short) = 190 single-probe scenarios, median 165 turns, ~3k tokens each; Set B (long) = 44 scenarios each with three fused probe threads, median 599 turns, 7-15k tokens each. Total graded probes = 322 (§4.3). Three domains (research papers, grocery/shopping, credit-card transactions).
construction: Synthetic with programmatic gold. Each scenario is a symbolic event program — a sequence of typed state operations (§4.1) — rendered into natural multi-session dialogue by a strong LLM (sonnet-4.6) (§4.3). Surface material grounded in real data (bioRxiv/arXiv papers, Instacart grocery dataset, synthetic credit-card transactions) but supplies "only vocabulary, never trap semantics." Gold answers computed by deterministic evaluator replay of the event program — no human-annotated gold (§4.3). Five failure modes designed in by construction: Status, Salience, Sequence, Compound, Anti-trap (§4.1).
human_validation: NO answer-level human validation of StateMemBench itself. Human annotation exists only for a cross-benchmark drift audit (Appendix A.4): 2 annotators (background not reported), 18 stratified cases from OTHER benchmarks (LongMemEval oracle, MemoryArena-shopping/search). Track A (structured, n=12): binary drift decision 83.3% raw agreement, kappa=0.43, PABAK=0.67; full-bucket label 50% raw, kappa=0.42. Track B (blind, n=6): kappa=0.80 on surface-level observation; all 12 blind free-text descriptions mapped onto existing buckets. Human-vs-judge: the two annotators assigned drift in only 58.3% and 41.7% of judge-flagged cases (both stricter than judge). Adjudication rule: "where exactly one family says drift we take the non-drift reading" (A.2). No attention/catch checks reported.
judge: Closed-pool grading: each probe has a constructed answer pool containing the gold, the drift target (superseded state), and 3-4 distractors; scores whether answer reflects current state, superseded state, or other failure (§4.3). Grading by DeepSeek-v4-pro LLM judge. Judge is NOT validated against human labels on StateMemBench answers — the only judge check is internal: a deterministic word-boundary matcher decides the 28% of answers naming exactly one pool option verbatim and agrees with the judge on 94.1% of those (Appendix C). Judge agreement numbers exist only for the separate cross-benchmark drift-labeling study: kappa=0.67 (LongMemEval), 91.6% raw / PABAK=0.83 (MemoryArena-shopping), and cross-family DeepSeek-vs-GPT-4o kappa=0.37 on LongMemEval oracle (Appendix A.3).
quality_controls: Programmatic verification that every load-bearing fact appears in its assigned session and no banned phrase leaks, with failing scenarios re-rendered (§4.3). Distractors built into every closed pool (gold + drift target + 3-4 distractors). Adversarial filter downgraded 32-47% of drift candidates during labeling (A.2); conservative non-drift adjudication when judge families disagree. Cross-model-family judge confirmation on external LongMemEval oracle. Contamination / parametric-knowledge-leak checks: ABSENT — no closed-book (no-context) control, no training-data contamination check. No ablation of the benchmark itself beyond the two length regimes.
splits: NONE reported — no dev/test split, no held-out set, no versioning policy. The two length regimes (Set A short / Set B long) are the only internal partition. Single run per configuration ("Each reported number is a single run per configuration," §6), temperature 0 with reasoning disabled; no multi-seed policy, no systematic error bars (Wilson 95% CIs appear only in the side-study on cross-benchmark drift prevalence, e.g. [30%, 60%] on LongMemEval oracle).
baselines: ~17 systems across four families (Table 3, §6.2): 5 memory systems (Mem0, A-Mem, LightMem, MemoryOS, StateMem), retrieval baselines (BM25, text-embedding-3-small), 4 graph-RAG (nano-graphrag, HippoRAG, LightRAG, GraphRAG), and long-context backbones (Qwen-3.5-9B, Qwen-3.6-35B, GPT-5.4-Nano, DeepSeek-V4-Flash). StateMem wrapper additionally tested across six backends (+32 to +67 points current-state accuracy).
cost_reporting: Essentially NONE for evaluated systems — no token budgets, dollar costs, or latency for baselines or the benchmark harness. Only cost fact reported: the StateMem wrapper's overhead over its matched control is "a fixed 155-token instruction and ≤250-word trace, both inside the one call" (§6.4), with a wrapper cost analysis referenced in Appendix F.5 (no $/latency numbers surfaced in main text).
release: NOT public as of 2026-08-28. Paper says "we release StateMemBench" (§4) and that the annotation kit (forms, keys, analyzer) "is released with the benchmark" (A.4), but provides NO URL, NO repository link, NO license, and NO datasheet anywhere (abstract, footnotes, appendices checked); web search finds no GitHub or HuggingFace page for StateMemBench. Paper accessible at arxiv.org/abs/2608.19652.
notable_practices: Practices this paper exemplifies that a new benchmark paper would be expected to match: (1) programmatic, deterministically verifiable gold labels (symbolic event program + evaluator replay) rather than annotated gold; (2) failure-mode taxonomy designed into construction (5 trap types incl. an Anti-trap control class); (3) closed-pool grading that separates "superseded-state" errors from generic wrong answers by construction; (4) automated consistency/leak verification with re-rendering of failing scenarios; (5) a deterministic-matcher cross-check on the LLM judge with a quantified agreement rate (94.1% on the 28% verbatim subset); (6) dual-track (structured + blind) human audit reporting kappa AND PABAK, plus a pre-registered conservative adjudication rule; (7) paired short/long length regimes to isolate length effects; (8) deterministic decoding (temp 0) stated explicitly. Its notable ABSENCES (single run per config, no judge-vs-human answer validation, no contamination check, no cost table, no release URL) are gaps a new benchmark can differentiate on.

paper: Neuromem: A Granular Decomposition of the Streaming Lifecycle in External Memory for LLMs (arXiv:2602.13967, Feb 2026; Ruicheng Zhang, Xinyi Li, Tianyi Xu, Shuhao Zhang, Xiaofei Liao, Hai Jin). A streaming-lifecycle testbed that benchmarks external memory modules under an interleaved insertion-and-retrieval protocol, decomposing the memory lifecycle into five dimensions: D1 Memory Data Structure, D2 Normalization (PreIns), D3 Consolidation (PostIns), D4 Query Formulation (PreRet), D5 Context Integration (PostRet) (Sec. 3.2).
scale: NO consolidated dataset-statistics table. Three source datasets serialized into chronological streams: LoCoMo ("10 core tasks, each comprising multiple sessions of multi-turn dialogue"), LongMemEval (Oracle subset; "N historical turns followed by a single query," N unspecified; multiple independent tasks concatenated into one chronological stream), and MemoryAgentBench (Selective Forgetting subset only; full benchmark excluded as static factual knowledge). Exact question counts, session counts, and tokens-per-stream are NOT stated anywhere in the paper.
construction: Hybrid/adapted rather than newly built: three existing benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MemoryAgentBench) are re-serialized into a continuous chronological stream R preserving temporal order, with insertions interleaved with retrievals during serving. Gold answers are inherited from the source benchmarks (paper notes LoCoMo carries "evidence labels that pinpoint the exact dialogue history required for reasoning"). No synthetic generation; the paper's own limitation section acknowledges "the scarcity of datasets explicitly curated for dynamic memory evolution precludes granular monitoring of intermediate states."
human_validation: NONE reported. No annotation protocol, no annotator counts, no kappa/percent agreement, no attention checks, no manual inspection or human-graded case studies anywhere in main text or appendices A-C.
judge: Purely automated scoring: token-level F1 with Porter stemming (plus latency metrics). NO LLM-as-judge is used anywhere (notably, it does not adopt LongMemEval's usual GPT-4-judge protocol), and consequently there is NO judge-vs-human validation — NONE reported. The LLMs in the paper (pangu-1b on Ascend 910B, Llama-3.1-8B on A6000, Qwen-Plus) are evaluated backbones, not judges.
quality_controls: No contamination or parametric-knowledge-leak checks (NONE reported); no distractor construction; no dev-set audits. What it does have: a controlled shared serving stack so only one lifecycle component varies at a time (a component-level ablation grid across D1-D5, e.g., Table 4: Property Graph + no consolidation F1 0.348→0.269 R1→R5 at <1 ms vs CRUD consolidation 0.351→0.273 at 3,777 ms); a backbone-robustness check swapping in Qwen-Plus (Sec. 5.3); identification of "latency traps" (e.g., Table 6: multi-query expansion spikes context-integration latency from <1 ms to ~1,700 ms with negligible F1 gain). These ablate the memory systems, not the benchmark data itself.
splits: No dev/test split, no held-out set. Instead a temporal checkpoint design: evaluation triggered at fixed intervals of the stream (e.g., every 20%), yielding five rounds R1-R5 that measure degradation as memory accumulates (Table 1: FIFO queue F1 0.169→0.094, -44.4%; Inverted+Vector 0.411→0.358, -12.9%). No multi-seed policy and no statistical significance tests reported.
baselines: 12 named memory systems mapped into the D1-D5 taxonomy (Sec. 4.2): TiM, MemoryBank, MemGPT, A-Mem, HippoRAG, HippoRAG 2, MemoryOS, LD-Agent, SCM, Mem0, Mem0g, SeCom — evaluated as interchangeable per-dimension variants within one shared serving stack rather than as end-to-end black boxes. Backbones: pangu-1b (Huawei Ascend 910B NPUs) and Llama-3.1-8B (Nvidia A6000 GPUs), plus Qwen-Plus as a robustness check (Sec. 5.3); E5-Large embeddings (Appendix C).
cost_reporting: Latency: yes, extensively — per-stage insertion latency, retrieval latency, and context-integration latency in ms (e.g., consolidation via CRUD costs 3,777 ms vs <1 ms for none; multi-query expansion ~1,700 ms), plus an "Intrinsic Efficiency Frontier" accuracy-vs-latency plot (Fig. 2) and F1-per-second trajectories per stage (Fig. 3). Dollar costs: NONE reported. Token counts of evaluated systems: NONE reported.
release: Claims to be an "open-source testbed" (abstract/contributions) but NO GitHub, HuggingFace, or anonymized-repo URL appears anywhere in the paper, and a web search surfaces no repository — release is claimed, not verifiable. arXiv page license: CC BY 4.0. No datasheet; documentation exists only as in-paper appendices A-C (implementation, algorithms, experimental workflows).
notable_practices: (1) Lifecycle decomposition with per-stage metric attribution — every accuracy/latency number is attributed to one of five pipeline stages rather than to a monolithic system; (2) degradation-over-time reporting: every result given as an R1→R5 trajectory with percent decline, not a single end-state score; (3) accuracy-vs-cost frontier plots and explicit "latency trap" callouts (high-cost components with negligible/negative accuracy gain); (4) controlled comparison via a unified serving stack so 12 systems' components are swapped one dimension at a time; (5) cross-backbone and cross-hardware robustness check (pangu-1b/Ascend vs Llama-3.1-8B/A6000 vs Qwen-Plus); (6) interleaved insertion-retrieval protocol itself, replacing ingest-then-query evaluation. Counter-examples for the gap analysis: no human validation, no judge validation, no contamination checks, no dataset statistics table, no statistical tests, and an unverifiable open-source claim.

paper: Veracium — "Ground Truth First: A Longitudinal Evaluation Instrument for Agent Memory, and the Tenure Crossover in Memory-Architecture Rankings" (arXiv:2607.21962, Quentin Spencer, submitted 2026-07-24, cs.CL)
scale: 383 validated questions across 15 question types (single-fact, inference-only, episodic, temporal, multi-session, knowledge-update current/past, preference current/application, expired-state, conflict-resolution, work-memory, abstention, abstention-false-premise, injection-probe) (§3.2). Two corpora: short horizon = 14 users / 275 validated questions, ~30-60 records per user (§2.3, §3.2); tenure corpus = 6 users with nine-week simulated histories, 108 questions instantiated as as-of-date sets at checkpoints weeks 3/6/9 (§3.2), n=324 judged answers per checkpoint cell (6 users x 3 replicates, §5.4). Read-stage context: 677 (vector) to 1,807 (hybrid v2) input tokens/question short-horizon; full rendered history ~2.8-5.2K tokens/question at week 9 (§5.8). 52,797 total LLM calls logged (34,076 original + 18,721 review-phase validation) (§3.4).
construction: Fully synthetic, fictionalized corpus, no real personal data (§3.1, Ethics). "Ground truth first" pipeline inverts the usual order: a seeded deterministic life-script sampler emits a timeline of facts per fictional user, each fact carrying a validity interval (when true), a volatility class, and a source channel — BEFORE any text is generated (§3.1). An LLM renderer (Amazon Nova Pro, deliberately a different model family from answerer and judge) turns each scripted event into a chat session or email against a per-event fact manifest (§3.1). Questions are instantiated mechanically from the script, never from rendered text, so gold answers are script-valid by construction (§3.1). A fidelity verifier checks every planted fact actually appears in the rendered text (§3.1). Fictionalization is explicitly motivated as an anti-pretraining-leak measure (citing frontier models scoring 70-85% closed-book on non-fictionalized benchmarks).
human_validation: Essentially NONE at benchmark-construction time: no human annotation protocol, no N annotators, no kappa/percent-agreement, no catch trials reported for item validation. Validation is model-based: following MemGym's protocol, an oracle LLM gets the complete rendered corpus open-book and must answer every generated question, scored by the judge — 215/220 questions validated (97.7%), 5 exclusions traced to a named oracle trust/recall tension over third-party-authored evidence (§3.3). Only human touchpoints: ~200 hand-spot-checked judge verdicts (3 errors caught; anecdotal, not a systematic protocol) and a blinded human adjudication pack described as "prepared" but deferred — "remains the arbiter for the judge-sensitive pair before archival submission" (§7). So human validation of both items and judge is acknowledged as pending, not done.
judge: LLM-as-judge: claude-sonnet-5 with a versioned rubric, treated as part of the benchmark definition and kept in a separate model family from the corpus generator (Nova Pro) (§3.4). NOT validated against human labels — zero human-agreement statistics reported; validation is cross-MODEL, not human: full re-judge with deepseek.v3.2 (different family) over 8,985 answers gives 87.9% agreement, Cohen's kappa=0.60 (§7). DeepSeek is systematically stricter (1,029 Sonnet-correct/DeepSeek-wrong vs 54 reverse); judge error correlates with answer style (verbosity, abstention wording). Headline crossover finding is reported under BOTH judges (+17.3 pp, p=0.063 primary; +24.1 pp, exact p=0.031 cross-family, §5.4). Human adjudication of the judge-sensitive comparison explicitly deferred to archival version (§7).
quality_controls: Parametric-leak control: no-memory (closed-book) arm scores 15.2% short-horizon and 16.0-16.7% tenure, bounding what model priors contribute (§3.4, §5.1); fully fictionalized entities to prevent pretraining contamination (§3.1). Injection probes: 14 unique planted injection questions (one per user) x 3 stochastic trials = 42 answer trials, built as six received-email attacks on a plausibility-graded ladder from absurd lottery to memory-poisoning directive, in a benign (non-adversarial-framing) harness (§3.2, §5.7). Fidelity verifier confirms every planted fact appears in rendered text (§3.1). Oracle answerability audit: 215/220 pass (97.7%), exclusions analyzed rather than discarded silently (§3.3). Also token-matched recency-window and full-history control arms to separate retrieval value from context-length effects (§5.8). No preregistration; hybrid v2 was designed after observing v1's failure on the same corpus — flagged by the author as a development-set number (§7).
splits: No conventional dev/test split. Held-out separation via generation order: the six long-horizon tenure users (new personas and preference chains) were generated AFTER hybrid v2 was frozen, so the tenure corpus functions as a held-out set relative to the architecture tuned on the short-horizon corpus (§7). Temporal checkpoint structure: weeks 3/6/9 as-of-date question sets (§3.2). Replication policy: every run repeated as 3 independent stochastic replicates (§3.4); corpus generator is seeded and deterministic, only LLM calls are stochastic (§3.4). Short-horizon results acknowledged as partially benchmark-informed iteration (Threats §7).
baselines: 5 memory architectures + 1 no-memory control, single answerer (claude-haiku-4-5-20251001, §3.4): (1) curated map, PEEK-shaped distill/cartograph/evict — 94.2% short (777/825), tenure 81.2%→78.4% wk3→wk9; (2) vector w/ Titan-v2 embeddings — 91.0%, 75.3%→74.7%; (3) typed labeled-property graph — 93.2%, 75.9%→90.4%; (4) hybrid v1 deterministic graph→map — 89.5%, below both parents (reported negative result, §5.2); (5) hybrid v2 layered (typed edges + episodes + wiki) — 96.8% (799/825), 80.2%→93.2%; (6) no-memory control 15.2%. Plus review-phase history baselines: full rendered history 97.9% short / 82.4-88.9% tenure; token-matched recency window 73.0% short / 42.9-66.4% long (§5.8). Core finding: tenure crossover — graph-vs-map ranking inverts with history length (+17.3 pp avg, 5/6 users positive, sign-flip p=0.063 primary judge; +24.1 pp, 6/6 users, exact p=0.031 cross-family judge, §5.4).
cost_reporting: Yes, unusually detailed. Read-stage: mean input tokens/question per architecture (677 vector to 1,807 hybrid v2 short-horizon; vector/hybrid grow +48-57% by week 9 while curated map stays flat at 1,183→1,182 tok/q); full history ~2.8-5.2K tok/q at week 9 (§5.8). Write-stage: curated writer spends ~4.6x the extractor's tokens (for 84.5% vs 74.6% fact recall). Dollar figure: ~$0.002/question answerer input at July-2026 list pricing (§5.8). Measurement cost itself reported: 52,797 total LLM calls, judging exceeded answering (15.0k vs 12.7k calls) — "half the instrument's spend is measurement" (§3.4). Latency: per-call wall-clock times shipped in released logs but not analyzed in the paper (§5.8).
release: Partially public at preprint time. GitHub https://github.com/veracium-ai/Veracium exists (public, MIT, ~7 stars, 1,032 commits) but is primarily the Veracium memory LIBRARY (pip install veracium) with docs at veracium-ai.github.io/Veracium; the benchmark artifacts per se — deterministic seeded corpus generator (MIT), synthetic corpus (CC BY 4.0), full harness with per-cell model configs and seeds, all judged verdicts from both judges, complete per-call logs with token counts — are promised in the Reproducibility statement as "in preparation... will accompany the archival version," i.e., not yet confirmed downloadable. No HuggingFace link found. LMSYS real-chat robustness corpus is license-gated and NOT redistributed; robustness tier ships synthetic fixtures. No formal datasheet reported; judge prompts versioned as part of the benchmark.
notable_practices: (1) Ground-truth-before-text generation with mechanical question instantiation, so gold labels are correct by construction rather than annotated post hoc. (2) Three-way model-family separation: corpus renderer (Nova Pro) vs answerer (Haiku 4.5) vs judge (Sonnet 5). (3) Judge versioned as part of the benchmark definition, plus full cross-family re-judge (8,985 answers, 87.9%, kappa=0.60) with headline claims reported under both judges. (4) Closed-book no-memory control quantifying parametric leakage (15.2%). (5) Cost as first-class output: per-architecture token tables, $/question, and disclosure that half the spend is measurement. (6) Exact paired McNemar tests, user-cluster bootstrap 95% CIs, sign-flip randomization and permutation tests (p<10^-4) — clustering by user, not by question. (7) Negative result (hybrid v1 below both parents) published with a named diagnosis. (8) Honest labeling of development-set vs held-out numbers and an 8-subsection threats-to-validity section that concedes the two weakest points (no human validation of the judge; benchmark-informed iteration). Gaps a new benchmark paper should avoid replicating: no human item annotation or agreement stats, judge never validated against humans (deferred), no preregistration, release incomplete at preprint.
